title: Best App to Store Rewards Cards: Top Picks 2026
summary: Find the best app to store rewards cards in 2026. Compare top options for keeping loyalty points organized, accessible, and easy to use on the go.
body_markdown:
Join Gerald for a new way to manage your finances.


Cash advances with no fees.


[Get Started](https://joingerald.com/#signup)


Apple Wallet is the easiest app to store rewards cards for iPhone users, Google Wallet is the direct pick for Android, and Catima is the best choice if you want **privacy focused, offline storage** without an account. That matters because U.S. consumers held an average of **19 loyalty program memberships** in 2024 but actively used only **9.3** , so the winning app is the one you'll open at checkout, not the one with the longest feature list.


Forget the popular advice to download one universal wallet and move everything into it. That approach fails when a retailer doesn't issue an official pass, when a barcode won't scan from a photo, or when you switch phones. Start with your device, then decide whether you need **official merchant passes** , manual card scanning, custom pass creation, offline access, or balance tracking.


This list separates those jobs clearly. You'll find built in wallets for speed, cross platform scanners for households that mix iPhone and Android, and niche tools for cards nobody else supports. Pick one primary wallet, add a backup only if you need it, and stop carrying a keychain full of plastic.

## 1. Apple Wallet


If you carry an iPhone, start here and only look elsewhere for cards Apple can't take.[Apple Wallet](https://www.apple.com/wallet/) is preinstalled, free, and built for fast access on **iPhone and Apple Watch** . You add most cards through **Add to Apple Wallet** links in retailer apps, emails, texts, or websites, not by scanning plastic yourself.


### What It Does Best


Location and time based prompts can surface the right pass near a store, and supported passes receive notifications and updates. That visibility matters, since mobile wallet research cited by RetailWire found **73% of respondents** were more likely to join a program when points were automatically updated and immediately visible, according to RetailWire's discussion of mobile wallets replacing plastic loyalty cards. Don't expect every independent shop to offer that level of integration.


- **Strengths:** Preinstalled, broad U.S. retailer support, strong security, and multiple barcode types.
- **Weaknesses:** Some retailers never issue Wallet passes, and manual pass creation is limited.
- **Best for:** iPhone users whose grocery, pharmacy, airline, and coffee programs already support Wallet.


If you're comparing Apple's payment tools with other options,[Gerald's comparison with Apple Pay Later](https://joingerald.com/gerald-vs-apple-pay-later) covers a different job than card storage. Keep Apple Wallet as your checkout layer, and use a tool like Pass2U only for the unsupported cards it leaves behind.


## 2. Google Wallet


Android users should make[Google Wallet](https://wallet.google/intl/en_us/) their default before trying third party scanners. It's free, works on Android phones and **Wear OS watches** , and stores loyalty cards, gift cards, tickets, transit passes, and payment cards in one place. Participating merchants can issue passes directly, while unsupported cards can sometimes be added manually for barcode or QR display.


The practical advantage is organization at scale. Forrester reported in 2024 that **85% of U.S. online adults** belonged to at least one retail loyalty program, a figure covered in[BCG's analysis of growing loyalty program expectations](https://www.bcg.com/publications/2024/loyalty-programs-customer-expectations-growing) . You're not solving a rare problem. You're managing programs you already joined and don't want to hunt for in separate retailer apps.


### Where It Falls Short


Merchant support still varies, and interface changes can bury loyalty passes among payment cards. Some cards require manual entry or a photo, which doesn't guarantee a scanner friendly result. Test each barcode once before you retire the plastic version.


- **Strengths:** Free, widely available, organized pass management, and retailer integrations across Google services.
- **Weaknesses:** Inconsistent merchant support and occasional manual workarounds.


For background on how digital payments fit together,[Gerald's guide to banking and payments](https://joingerald.com/learn/banking--payments) is useful context. For rewards cards specifically, Google Wallet is the Android baseline every other app must beat.


## 3. Samsung Wallet


Galaxy owners don't need to choose between Samsung and Google immediately. Samsung Wallet stores membership and loyalty cards with barcode display alongside payment cards, tickets, keys, and some regional IDs. Its tight integration with Galaxy hardware and **biometric security** makes it feel native in a way third party wallets can't match on Samsung phones.


Use it if you already live in Samsung's ecosystem and want memberships next to your other wallet items. Cash back features add value for some shoppers, though they aren't a reason to switch phones. It can also run alongside Google Wallet, so you can keep official Google passes in one place and Samsung specific items in the other without conflict.


**Practical rule:** Don't maintain the same card in two wallets long term. Pick the one you open fastest and delete the duplicate.


The trade offs are clear. Features vary by market, it works best on Samsung devices, and fewer retailers offer an **Add to Samsung Wallet** option than they do for Apple or Google. If you plan to leave Galaxy hardware soon, Google Wallet is the safer primary choice. If you're staying, Samsung Wallet is a perfectly defensible default.


## 4. Key Ring


Choose[Key Ring](https://web.keyringapp.com/) when your built in wallet won't accept half your cards and you shop for groceries every week. This free iOS and Android app scans and stores cards from a large retail database, including membership and library cards that official wallets often ignore. You show the barcode at checkout and skip the physical keychain tags entirely.


### More Than Card Storage


Key Ring adds **weekly ads, circulars, and shareable shopping lists** on top of card storage. That's either useful or clutter, depending on how you shop. Grocery planners who check circulars before a trip will use those tools. Minimalists who only want a barcode in two taps will find them distracting and should pick Catima or mobile-pocket instead.


Cloud backup and cross device synchronization protect your cards when you replace a phone, but full backup and sharing require a cloud account. That's a reasonable trade if convenience matters more than keeping data strictly on device. Households sharing one grocery card across two phones benefit most.


- **Strengths:** Mature U.S. retail coverage, easy scanning, and useful grocery features.
- **Weaknesses:** Advertising and shopping content you may never open.


Key Ring earns its place as the cross platform scanner for everyday retail, not as a replacement for official passes that update balances automatically.


## 5. mobile-pocket loyalty cards


For a clean cross platform wallet without grocery circulars,[mobile-pocket](https://www.mobile-pocket.com/en/) is the better pick. It's free on iOS and Android, includes an **Apple Watch companion** , and lets you add cards by scanning them or searching a broad global catalog. Cards sync between devices through the cloud, so a phone upgrade doesn't mean rescanning everything.


That watch access is a real differentiator at self checkout. Pulling a barcode up on your wrist beats opening a phone with full hands. In app merchant offers are present, but they don't dominate the interface the way shopping content can in other wallets. Active development also matters, since abandoned card apps become a migration headache.


The global catalog cuts both ways. Travelers and people with non U.S. programs get coverage that U.S. only apps lack. Occasional localization prompts remind you the catalog spans many markets, and merchant promotions won't appeal to everyone. Neither issue slows down barcode display, which is the core job.


- **Strengths:** Clean interface, large program catalog, watch support, and cross platform sync.
- **Weaknesses:** Promotions and localization quirks tied to global coverage.


If you're evaluating unrelated payment services,[Gerald's comparison with Doxo](https://joingerald.com/gerald-vs-doxo) addresses bill pay rather than loyalty storage. For a household mixing iPhone and Android, mobile-pocket is the most balanced shared choice on this list.


## 6. FidMe


Pick[FidMe](https://app.fidme.com/) if you're migrating from an older card wallet or your cards live in screenshots and email threads. This free iOS and Android app imports loyalty cards from **screenshots, emails, and other wallets** , which saves tedious rescanning when you switch apps. It also digitizes receipts and warranties, plus coupons, weekly deals, and expense tracking.


That breadth explains both its appeal and its main drawback. A neutral survey of 1,000 smartphone users found **33% had used mobile wallets** for non payment functions like storing coupons or loyalty cards, as reported in[Retail Dive's coverage of retailers lagging on mobile wallet loyalty](https://www.retaildive.com/ex/mobilecommercedaily/retailers-lag-on-coupon-loyalty-opportunities-with-mobile-wallets-report) . FidMe targets exactly that non payment use case and bundles more of it than most rivals.


### Who Should Skip It


If you want a two tap barcode and nothing else, the all in one interface will feel busy. Coupon availability varies by region, and some in app features vary as well. You may spend time ignoring sections you'll never use.


- **Strengths:** Strong import tools and receipt organization in the same app as your cards.
- **Weaknesses:** Busier interface than minimalist wallets, with regional gaps in deals.


FidMe makes sense for organized shoppers who want cards, receipts, and warranties together. Everyone else should choose a lighter wallet.


## 7. WalletPasses | Passbook Wallet


[WalletPasses](https://walletpasses.io/) solves one specific problem, and solves it well. Retailers and event organizers often send passes in Apple's **PKPASS format** , which Android's built in tools don't always handle cleanly. This free Android app opens and manages those files, organizing loyalty cards, coupons, and tickets and displaying their barcodes when you need them.


Don't choose it as your primary scanner for plastic cards. It depends on pass issuers providing files in the first place, and some fields or images may not transfer perfectly into the Android view. It also offers fewer deal discovery features than ad supported wallets, which most users will count as a benefit rather than a loss.


A pass file viewer and a card scanner are different tools. Buying one to do the other's job leads to frustration at checkout.


Import and export options make it easier to move passes between devices or keep copies. That matters for people who receive work, travel, or event passes by email on a computer and need them on a phone later.


- **Strengths:** Focused, lightweight handling of Apple format passes on Android.
- **Weaknesses:** No issuer pass means nothing to store, and rendering isn't always perfect.


Keep WalletPasses as a utility next to Google Wallet if PKPASS files show up in your inbox regularly.


## 8. Pass2U Wallet


When a gym, library, or local shop gives you a barcode but no official wallet pass,[Pass2U Wallet](https://www.pass2u.net/) is the workaround. Available on iOS and Android, it lets you **create custom passes** from a barcode or card number, then use them with Apple Wallet and Google Wallet. It also manages and imports PKPASS files.


### Creation Takes Patience


Building a pass means choosing templates, entering numbers correctly, and testing the result at a scanner. First time users often find that process fiddly, and some advanced features require in app purchases. Budget ten minutes per card, not thirty seconds, and verify each pass before you leave the physical card at home.


The merchant side is a separate reason to know this tool. Its optional platform gives businesses cloud tools, APIs, and pass updates, so a small retailer can issue proper wallet passes without building its own app. That doesn't change your checkout experience directly, but it explains why the app handles pass structure more seriously than simple scanners.


- **Strengths:** Creates passes for cards with no official support, across both major platforms.
- **Weaknesses:** Fiddly setup and paid advanced features.


Use Pass2U to fill gaps in Apple Wallet or Google Wallet. Don't use it to rebuild cards that already have official passes.


## 9. Catima Loyalty Card Wallet


[Catima](https://catima.app/) is my recommendation for anyone who distrusts cloud accounts. This free, **open source Android app** stores unlimited loyalty and membership cards on your device, works fully offline, and requires no login. You scan or enter barcodes, open the card at checkout, and that's the entire experience. No ads, no merchant network, no deals feed.


Offline access isn't a minor detail. Mobile wallet research reported that **43% of consumers** failed to use loyalty cards because they didn't bring the physical card, a finding linked earlier in this guide. A barcode that loads without a signal in a basement grocery store solves that failure directly. Catima also imports from FidMe, Loyalty Card Keychain, and files, supports some PKPASS files, and offers optional Wear OS integration.


### The Privacy Trade Off


There's no built in cloud backup. If you lose your phone without your own backup approach, you rescan everything. That's the honest cost of keeping data on device, and privacy focused users should accept it knowingly rather than complain later.


- **Strengths:** Open source, ad free, lightweight, fast, and account free.
- **Weaknesses:** No coupons, deals, balances, or automatic backup.


For pure card storage on Android, nothing on this list is cleaner. iPhone users can't use it, which is its only structural limit.


## 10. AwardWallet


[AwardWallet](https://awardwallet.com/) isn't a checkout barcode app, and judging it as one misses its purpose. This iOS, Android, and web service consolidates **points, miles, elite status, and expiration dates** across hundreds of programs, with a clear strength in travel rewards. It answers how much you have and when you'll lose it, not how to scan a grocery card.


Expiration alerts and balance monitoring justify it for frequent travelers managing airline, hotel, and credit card programs. Family and account sharing help households track rewards together, and CSV export suits people who keep their own records. Industry coverage notes **72% of surveyed loyalty members** actively use one to three programs, according to[EPAM's report on consumers choosing how they earn rewards](https://www.epam.com/about/newsroom/in-the-news/2025/81-percent-of-consumers-want-to-pick-how-they-earn-choose-rewards) . If your active list is longer than that, tracking stops being optional.


The security consideration is real. AwardWallet requires connecting accounts, so you're trusting a third party with credential aggregation. Users uncomfortable with that model should skip it and check balances manually. A free tier exists, while **AwardWallet Plus** is paid with pricing subject to change.


- **Strengths:** Broad travel program coverage, expiration alerts, and status tracking.
- **Weaknesses:** Not designed for grocery or drugstore barcode scanning.


Pair it with Apple Wallet or Google Wallet. One tracks value, the other gets you through checkout.
